candidates.title: Engineering AI Discover
candidates.summary: The challenges and decisions behind AI Discover’s intelligence layer By Varun Khaitan , Peng Ren , Gary Tang , Itay Teller , Atif Faheem , Nipun Kumar , Donnie DeBoer , Eduardo Lundgren , Matteo Rinaldi , Raghav Bakshi We recently introduced AI Discover , a new tab in our TV app where a small group of members can try new ways to find something to watch. For years, our recommendations have worked in the background, inferring what a member might enjoy from their viewing history. AI Discover moves from that silent ranking toward steerable discovery. A member picks a theme, say “Quick Watches,” and gets a row of matching titles, a short note on why they fit and a few narrower themes to try next. From there, they can keep narrowing, head somewhere new or tune what they see. Building AI Discover raised a question many teams will recognize: how do you deliver a better member experience with generative AI on TV without sacrificing speed, reliability or safety? Our answer is a new intelligence layer, the agent harness behind AI Discover. For each request, it decides how to combine LLMs with our recommendation systems. It builds on years of work understanding what members enjoy, and on our recent work applying LLMs to recommendations and generative experiences. The layer itself plans each request, runs it across those systems, serves the result and evaluates it offline. candidates.title: Smooth Cruiser at Lyft: Built for Safety and Transparency
candidates.summary: At Lyft, we want to ensure everyone on the Lyft platform is supported by smart, fair tools to improve their experience. This is the guiding principle behind Smooth Cruiser, our feature that provides Drivers with insights into their driving behavior. For a tool like this to truly help Drivers make informed decisions for themselves, it must excel in two areas: real-world scoring and increased transparency into how that score is determined. Safety scoring often relies on fixed thresholds — a single cutoff applied to every Driver, on every road, in every market. This method fails to account for the dynamic reality of driving. A harsh brake on a quiet local road is fundamentally different from a sudden stop in city traffic. Drivers need a system that recognizes these nuances. Smooth Cruiser recognizes these nuances and is built on two principles: a) score that reflects real world conditions, and b) transparency. In Part 1, we break down how the scoring works — how every signal is measured relative to local conditions, how Drivers are benchmarked against peers in structurally similar markets, and how a rolling window captures typical behavior rather than isolated moments. In Part 2, we walk through how we brought that methodology to the surface — giving Drivers direct visibility into the data behind their score, ride by ride, so they can understand it, act on it, and provide top-notch service to Riders. candidates.summary: Rebuilding Guardian: How Pinterest Upgraded Its Real-Time Abuse Platform to Modern Infrastructure at Scale Authors : Sharon Xie, Sr. Staff Software Engineer | Zhenxiao Luo, Sr Staff Software Engineer |Yi Pan, Principal Software Engineer | Vikram Deshpande, Sr. Engineering Manager Guardian helps Pinterest teams turn real-time event data into meaningful insights and operational outcomes. It enables subject matter experts to analyze real-time event streams, identify evolving patterns, and operationalize those learnings through signals, policies, and downstream workflows. Over the years, Guardian has supported a wide range of use cases, including spam and fraud response, account takeover detection, risk monitoring, and unsafe content enforcement. As Pinterest scaled, however, the original Guardian platform began to reach its limits. To meet growing demands around scale, reliability, and compliance, we rebuilt the system as Guardian V2 on top of modern data infrastructure. In this blog series, we’ll share our journey in building the next generation of Guardian, or Guardian V2. In this first part, we’ll discuss the challenges we faced, the architecture shift, and the foundational decisions that improved the platform’s reliability, scalability and compliance alignment. candidates.title: How Pinterest Improved Analytics Agent Compliance with Loop Engineering
candidates.summary: Skyler Zheng | Software Engineer II; Chris Moradi | Staff Data Scientist; Lu Liu | Staff Software Engineer; Aman Gairola | Manager II; Michael Chau | Manager II The Compliance Problem Compliance means following the right steps at the right time Pinterest’s Analytics Agent helps teams answer questions such as “How did query latency for the ads reporting pipeline change last week?” It searches the company’s data ecosystem, analyzes the relevant information, and recommends an answer or course of action. Not every question requires the same steps. We call the agent compliant when it identifies and follows the steps that apply. Improving compliance is intended to make answers more consistent and reduce the risk of incomplete or inaccurate results. Examples include: Read the data-discovery skill when it needs help finding the right tools or sources. Inspect table metadata before writing SQL to learn what the columns mean, which filters are required, and whether the table has important usage notes. Search every relevant source type , including tables, dashboards, and metrics, rather than stopping at the first useful result. These are three examples from a broader set of compliance rules, and whether they apply depends on the question. If a user provides the appropriate table, the agent may not need the data-discovery skill, while an open-ended question may require a broader search. candidates.title: Beyond Test Cards: A Fake Payment Provider for Testing at Scale
candidates.summary: Image generated with Google Gemini, 2026 Written by Savelii Kolesnikov , Jay Patel , and Ivanna Sivak Background Lyft processes billions in payments annually, and that volume continues to grow. Agentic coding has drastically accelerated feature development, but it raises the stakes for the one phase that cannot be rushed: ensuring the highest standards of reliability and correctness in critical payment systems. Every payment platform eventually hits the same wall. Unit tests cover business rules, integration tests validate boundaries, and load tests push upstream limits, but standard testing stops the moment a request reaches a third-party processor. Processor test cards are built for simple flows: a card either passes every payment action, from authorization to capture to refund, or fails them all. Real payment flows often have one step fail while the others succeed. In this post, we’ll explain why test cards break down and how we built our own fake payment provider to simulate any processor behavior on demand. Unlike a typical mock, it runs safely in production, so we can load test our payment stack and trial new workflows on simulated riders before real ones. Test cards don’t get you there with rideshare Unlike paying for a product on an e-commerce website or your favorite streaming platform, Lyft, as a rideshare company, has a unique set of challenges with payments.
